column1: # OWASP ZAP baseline rule configuration for the DAFS API.
# Format: <rule id>
# Actions: WARN (report, do not fail), IGNORE (do not report), FAIL.
# Every IGNORE here is a deliberate decision with a reason, not a way to get a
# green run. An alert that is genuinely inapplicable to this surface is noise
# that trains the reader to skim; an alert that is applicable stays.
# The daemon binds loopback and is unauthenticated by design — see the daemon's
# --listen default and dafs_api::logging. That pairing is documented, so the
# alerts that restate it are ignored. What this scan is actually looking for is
# the accidental kind: a reflected parameter, a header leaking a filesystem
# path, a crash on a malformed query.
# If the bind address is ever widened, revisit this entire file: most of the
# reasoning below stops holding the moment the API is reachable off-host.
# Content Security Policy. The UI is a single self-contained page with inlined
# script and style, which is what makes the daemon one deployable artifact; a
# meaningful CSP for it would need hashes regenerated on every build. Worth
# doing when the page loads anything it did not ship with — today it does not.

column3: CSP header not set — single self-contained page, revisit if it ever loads external content

column1: # Anti-clickjacking / X-Frame-Options. Framing a loopback-only page that
# displays the local user's own file listing to that same local user is not a
# meaningful attack path.

column3: Loopback-only UI; framing yields nothing the viewer cannot already see

column1: # X-Content-Type-Options. Every response sets an explicit Content-Type, so
# sniffing has nothing to guess at. Cheap to add regardless — tracked, not
# ignored.

column3: Explicit Content-Type on every route; worth adding the header anyway

column1: # HTTPS-related alerts. The API is plain HTTP on loopback deliberately: TLS to
# 127.0.0.1 protects against nothing and would require a certificate the daemon
# has no way to obtain. Peer traffic from M05 onward is a separate surface and
# is mutually authenticated and encrypted from its first line of code.

column3: HSTS is meaningless on a loopback HTTP listener
Permissions-Policy: no browser feature is used by this page

column1: # Cache headers. The timeline is local, non-sensitive to the local user, and
# already refetched every five seconds by the page itself.

column3: Local-only content, polled continuously; caching directives add nothing

column1: # Information disclosure via the server banner. Worth knowing about if it ever
# starts reporting a version, so this stays a warning rather than an ignore.

column3: Watch for a version-bearing Server header

column1: # Timestamp disclosure. /version and /metrics report uptime and event
# timestamps because that is their purpose.

column3: Timestamps are the intended content of /version and /metrics
